description: Expanded data on the security of Chinese assets in the DRC: specific PSCs, scale, incidents, official police/military cooperation.
verification_status: the structure and company names are confirmed by industry sources (Africa Center, Carnegie, Military Africa); presence in the DRC specifically is confirmed, but headcounts at specific DRC sites are not publicly disclosed - estimates are drawn by analogy with other BRI countries.

nature_of_chinese_pscs.key_distinction_from_the_west: Chinese PSCs are formally called 'private', but are in fact state-licensed entities accountable to the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Public Security. Of roughly 5,000 registered security firms in China, only 20 are licensed to operate abroad.
nature_of_chinese_pscs.functions: perimeter security, cargo escort, training local guards, intelligence-sharing with the host ministry; unlike Wagner, they do NOT take part in combat operations and do not act as political security advisers.
nature_of_chinese_pscs.weapons: a gray area - Chinese law tightly regulates weapons domestically but does not require a license for overseas operations; the matter is left to the host country's discretion.

companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.name: DeWe Security Service (Beijing Dewei Baoan Fuwu, 北京德威保安服务)
companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.status: the most visible and frequently cited company; per Carnegie Endowment and Grey Dynamics, officially operates in the DRC, Cameroon, Chad, Nigeria, Djibouti, and Ethiopia
companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.founders: former military and police officers who had worked together at the 2008 Beijing Olympics
companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.staff: 352 full-time Chinese staff abroad plus about 3,000 locally hired staff (globally, early 2020s data); has trained 70,000-86,000 contractors since 2013
companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.regional_clients: China Road and Bridge Corporation, CNPC, China National Petroleum, China Development Bank - all of which also have DRC projects

companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.name: Huaxin Zhong An Security Group
companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.status: one of three companies licensed to carry weapons abroad; specializes in maritime escort (Gulf of Guinea, Gulf of Aden) but also guards facilities
companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.scale: together with DeWe, about 35,000 contractors across 50 countries in Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East

companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.name: Shandong Huawei / Haiwei Security Group
companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.status: per the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, specializes specifically in guarding Chinese mines in southern Africa

companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.name: China Security Technology Group, VSS Security Group
companies_confirmed_active_in_the_drc.status: listed among the 20 companies licensed for overseas operations; in Sudan and South Sudan they accompany local armed forces on operations - the most 'permissive' operating model

scale_in_context.estimated_real_number: significantly higher than the official figure, according to researchers (Paul Nantulya, Africa Center)
scale_in_context.comparison_with_pla: the combined PSC contractor headcount exceeds the 2,500 PLA personnel stationed across the entire African continent (including peacekeepers and the Djibouti base)
scale_in_context.chinese_state_company_security_spending: ≈$10bn/year worldwide (estimate by the China Overseas Security and Defense Research Center)

documented_incidents_around_facility_sec.event: AFREWATCH has documented at least 35 cases of physical violence/torture against artisanal miners who entered mine sites in southern DRC
a viral video: two artisanal miners beaten by guards at the COMMUS (Zijin) mine in Kolwezi for entering the pit area
roughly 10,000 artisanal miners forcibly evicted from the Tenke Fungurume site
attack on a gold mine (Ituri/South Kivu): 2 Chinese nationals, a Congolese woman, and a Ugandan killed; 10 more Chinese workers reported missing
ambush on a mining convoy in Lamba village, Fizi, South Kivu: 2 Chinese, 1 Ghanaian, and 1 Congolese soldier killed
attack on a Chinese gold concession in Fizi: 2 Chinese nationals and a Ghanaian interpreter killed; the site's security at the time of the attack was provided by FARDC soldiers, not a private company
documented_incidents_around_facility_sec.significance: direct documentary confirmation that protection of Chinese sites in the east is often assigned to the DRC's own armed forces rather than Chinese PSCs

signatories: Jacquemain Shabani Lukoo Bihango (DRC Deputy PM, Interior Ministry)
Wang Xiaohong (Chinese State Councillor, Minister of Public Security)
2026_police_agreement.content: Chinese technical assistance to the DRC's National Police (PNC) on three fronts: organized crime, mining fraud, cybercrime; a joint working group was set up
2026_police_agreement.significance: the first agreement of its kind at the police (not military) level; it expands China's footprint in the DRC's security space without directly deploying the PLA or a PMC

direct_military_assistance.format: arms supplies (CH-4 drones, negotiations on Wing Loong 2 and fighter jets) - see military_dimension.json; there are no official reports of PLA units being stationed in the DRC
direct_military_assistance.regional_comparison: China's first-ever defense attache in Africa was only posted (to Niger) in February 2025 - a sign that even routine military-diplomatic presence on the continent remains limited and new
direct_military_assistance.pla_base: the PLA's only overseas base in Africa is in Djibouti (since 2017); there is no comparable facility in the DRC

why_there_is_no_second_wagner.thesis: Beijing systematically avoids overt military involvement because: (1) the official non-interference doctrine remains diplomatically valuable; (2) the risk of neo-colonialism accusations is already rising alongside the growing number of human-rights complaints (see human_rights_legal.json); (3) the economic model already works through control of processing and capital rather than military control of territory.
why_there_is_no_second_wagner.caveat: the police-cooperation agreement (May 2026) and the growing number of security contracts show the threshold is gradually shifting - but toward policing and security, not combat operations.
